typical: put the clock forward. NOT for: back.
Put the clocks forward one hour.
We put our watches forward.
put in: verb
fix equipment in place so that it can be used
typical: put in a bathroom/heating/a new kitchen. NOT for: taking things out.
We had a new bathroom put in.
They put in a new heating system.
verb
spend time or energy on a job
typical: put in effort/hours/work. NOT for: wasting time.
She put in a lot of hard work.
He puts in long hours at the office.
verb
interrupt a conversation to say something
typical: put in a word, 'I'm sixteen too,' she put in. NOT for: saying nothing.
'I'm sixteen too,' she put in.
Let me just put in a word here.
verb
make an official request or claim
typical: put in a claim/an order/an application. NOT for: accepting requests.
We must put in an order by tonight.
She put in for a pay rise.
verb
do something in a particular way, especially a performance
typical: put in a great performance/an appearance. NOT for: private activities.
He put in a brilliant performance.
The prime minister put in an appearance at the party.
put off: verb
delay something until a later time
typical: put off a decision/a meeting/doing sth. NOT for: cancelling it.
They put off the wedding until June.
Don't put off going to the dentist.
verb
make someone dislike something or lose interest
typical: put sb off (sth/doing sth). NOT for: delaying.
The smell put me off my food.
Bad reviews put people off the film.
verb
distract someone so they cannot concentrate
typical: put sb off (their game/work). NOT for: making someone dislike.
Stop talking, you'll put me off.
The noise put the speaker off.
verb
make someone leave a bus or train (BrE)
typical: put sb off (at a stop). NOT for: delaying.
The driver put him off at the next stop.
They were put off the train for having no ticket.
put on: verb
place clothes, shoes, make-up or glasses on your body
typical: put on a coat/shoes/make-up/sun cream. NOT for: switching on a machine.
Put on your coat, it's cold.
She put on some lipstick.
verb
switch on a device, or start playing music or a film
typical: put the light/TV/kettle on, put a CD on. NOT for: dressing.
Put the kettle on, please.
He put on some music.
verb
increase in weight
typical: put on weight/two kilos. NOT for: adding clothes.
I've put on a few kilos this winter.
She had put on weight since last year.
verb
organize or present a show, event or exhibition
typical: put on a play/concert/exhibition. NOT for: wearing something.
The students put on a play at the end of term.
The museum put on a new exhibition.
verb
pretend to have a feeling or way of speaking
typical: put on an act/an accent/a show. NOT for: real feelings.
She put on a brave smile.
He put on a fake accent to impress them.
verb
provide an extra bus, train or service
typical: put on extra trains/buses. NOT for: starting a show.
The railway put on extra trains for the match.
They put on a special bus for the festival.
verb
add an amount, cost or tax to something
typical: put sth on the price/bill. NOT for: gaining weight.
The government put 5p on a pack of cigarettes.
The hotel put a charge on the bill.
verb
bet money on something
typical: put money on a horse/a team. NOT for: investing in a business.
He put £20 on the favourite.
She put money on England to win.
verb
put cream, make-up or lotion on your skin
typical: put sth on (your skin/face). NOT for: taking off.
I put sun cream on before going out.
She put some lipstick on.
verb
do something that affects or influences someone or something
typical: put a limit/pressure/a tax on sth. NOT for: removing.
The government put a limit on imports.
Pat was putting pressure on him to leave.
put out: verb
make a fire stop burning
typical: put out a fire/a cigarette. NOT for: lighting.
Firefighters put out the fire.
He put out his cigarette.
verb
make a light stop working
typical: put the light out. NOT for: switching on.
Put the light out before you go to bed.
She put out the candles.
verb
place things where people can find and use them
typical: put out cups/food/chairs. NOT for: hiding.
She put out the cups and plates.
He put out some chairs for guests.
verb
feel upset or offended
typical: be/feel put out. NOT for: happy.
We were put out at not being invited.
She felt a little put out.
verb
cause extra work or trouble for someone
typical: put sb out. NOT for: helping.
I hope it won't put you out.
I don't want to put you out.
verb
make an effort to help someone
typical: put yourself out (for sb). NOT for: relaxing.
They put themselves out to entertain her.
She put herself out for her guests.
verb
take something outside your home and leave it there
typical: put the rubbish/cat out. NOT for: bringing inside.
Remember to put the cat out.
He put the rubbish out.
verb
publish or release something such as a statement or report
typical: put out a statement/a book. NOT for: private use.
The company put out a statement.
The group put out a new album.
put over: succeed in telling others your ideas or feelings (BrE)
typical: put sth over. NOT for: confusing.
The advert puts over the message clearly.
She put her view over well.
deceive someone (put one over on sb, informal)
typical: put one over on sb. NOT for: telling the truth.
Nobody could put one over on him.
They tried to put one over on us.
put through: verb
connect someone on the telephone
typical: put sb through (to sb). NOT for: cutting off.
Could you put me through to Eddie?
I'll put you through.
verb
pay for someone to go to school or university
typical: put sb through college. NOT for: refusing.
His parents put him through university.
She put herself through school.
verb
make someone experience something unpleasant
typical: put sb through sth. NOT for: sparing.
I'm sorry I put you through that.
They put her through a lot.
verb
get a plan or law officially approved
typical: put sth through. NOT for: blocking.
The government put the bill through.
They put through the new rules.
put together: prepare or produce something by collecting pieces
typical: put sth together. NOT for: taking apart.
It took all morning to put the proposal together.
typical: put sth together. NOT for: dismantling.
put up: verb
build or fix something in place
typical: put up a fence/tent/building. NOT for: taking something down.
They're putting up new office blocks.
We put up the tent before dark.
verb
fix something on a wall or surface for people to see
typical: put up a poster/notice/picture. NOT for: building walls.
She put up a notice in the hall.
He put up some shelves in the kitchen.
verb
raise something, such as your hand or a price
typical: put up your hand/prices/taxes. NOT for: lowering.
The shop put up its prices again.
Put up your hand if you know.
verb
let someone stay in your home for a short time
typical: put sb up for the night. NOT for: building something.
We can put you up for the weekend.
A friend put me up while I looked for a flat.
verb
show or try hard against someone or something
typical: put up a fight/resistance/an argument. NOT for: giving up.
The team put up a good fight.
He put up little resistance.
verb
provide money for a plan or a project
typical: put up money/the cash/a reward. NOT for: receiving money.
A bank put up the money for the project.
The family put up a reward.
put up with: accept an unpleasant situation or person without complaining
typical: put up with sb/sth. NOT for: complaining.
She put up with his temper.
I can't put up with the noise.
